defaults.permitted_development: Across Somerset, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Across Somerset, a roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Across Somerset, depth is controlled by projection from the roof plane rather than by the size of the opening alone. Once the unit projects more than 150mm, the straightforward householder route is usually lost.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Somerset, roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Across Somerset, roof-lights are treated as minor roof alterations, not full roof enlargements, so the existing roof form should remain dominant. Roof terraces, raised platforms and larger roof additions sit outside the normal roof-light route.
rules.materials_rules: Across Somerset, choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building roof usually needs a heritage-led approach: even a small roof-light can require consent if it affects the historic fabric or appearance.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or earlier planning condition can take away the normal roof-light permitted development route, particularly on prominent roof slopes.

rules.permitted_development: In Bath and North East Somerset, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: The roof-light should not make any part of the roof higher than it is now. A low-profile installation that leaves the original roof form dominant is generally the strongest option.
rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Installing roof-lights in a listed building, or altering historic roof fabric within its curtilage, can require listed building consent even where the unit looks modest.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the standard roof-light allowance survives everywhere: Article 4 controls and site-specific conditions can require an application for visible roof changes.

rules.permitted_development: In North Somerset, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: Keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required for roof-lights where the work alters historic roof fabric, framing, coverings or the character of the building.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or earlier planning condition can take away the normal roof-light permitted development route, particularly on prominent roof slopes.
